newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada agrees to help troubled Canadian Airlines.
newsitem.headline: Canada agrees to help troubled Canadian Airlines.

text.p: Canadian Transport Minister David Anderson said on Wednesday Canada and two provincial governments had agreed to a one-month delay in repayments of capital from troubled Canadian Airlines.

He also said the federal government would seriously examine any proposal by AMR Corp., parent of the American Airlines, to increase its minority shareholding in Canadian, though it would not necessarily agree to allow it.
"The federal government along with many other creditors has been asked for a delay in repayment in capital," Anderson told reporters.
Canadian has C$30 million ($22.5 million) left of the original $C120 million ($90 million) in loan guarantees provided by Canada and the governments of Alberta and British Columbia, he said
"They simply asked us to slide that for a month. They'll continue to pay interest. We're quite willing to accede to that, as have the other two governments involved," he said.
Other creditors have acted similarly, Anderson added.

Canadian said Friday it was in financial trouble, and would seek a 10-percent wage cut from its 16,400 employees and a cut in reservation and computer managment fees paid to Fort Worth, Tex.-based AMR as part of a sweeping survival plan.

AMR said it had no plans to increase its investment in Canadian, but if it wanted to it would require federal exemption from a rule limiting non-Canadian ownership of Canadian airlines' voting shares to 25 percent.
AMR has a 25 percent voting interest and 33 percent total stake in Canadian.
Anderson, asked if Ottawa would agree to raise the limit for AMR, said the question was hypothetical since no request had been made.
But he added, "Of course a serious proposal from any airline would be looked at seriously. It doesn't mean to say we'd accept it."
Canadian said on Wednesday it had no plans to ask AMR to up its stake in the ailing carrier.
"It's not even being considered at this point," said Canadian's Claudia Cattaneo.

However, Canadian would favour being allowed to attract more U.S. investors, something currently prohibited by regulations that say non-Canadian investors cannot hold more than 25 percent of its voting shares, Cattaneo said.

Canadian officials also reiterated that, despite a call for a government bailout from the airline's major unions, the company was not preparted to ask for more public money to help it dig out of a possible cash crunch.
